source_review.notes: Checked current RFC Editor publications for TCP, blind-attack hardening, initial sequence generation, high-performance extensions, retransmission timing, congestion control, SYN-flood mitigations and TIME-WAIT behavior, plus current Linux TCP sysctl documentation. All ten cited URLs returned HTTP 200 after normal redirects; normative protocol rules, Linux controls, abstract models, operational guidance and assurance remain separately scoped.

evidence: Checked connection tuple, protocol state, send and receive sequence spaces, windows, ownership, timers, queues, errors, accounting, lifetime and generation notation.
Reviewed modular ordering, segment sequence length, ACK bounds, receive-window acceptability, listener limits, reference sums and timer generations.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation separates connection identity, incarnation, protocol guards, queued resources, asynchronous timer work and object lifetime.

evidence: Executed six guarded active-open and active-close transitions from CLOSED through SYN-SENT, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2 and TIME-WAIT.
Confirmed each transition requires the expected predecessor and the sequence terminates in CLOSED.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The deterministic computation validates one abstract state path only; it implements no TCP packet, sequence validation, timer, retransmission, kernel socket, peer or concurrency.

evidence: Re-derived modular before ordering for differences below half the 32-bit sequence space and inclusion of SYN and FIN in segment length.
Checked ACK bounds, separate SYN and accept capacities, hierarchical byte accounting, reference exhaustion and timer-generation guards.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The relations are subsystem reasoning tools and do not claim a complete formalization of TCP, Linux connection tables, application APIs or all modular edge cases.

evidence: Reviewed active, passive and simultaneous open, duplicate SYN, lost SYN-ACK, reordered final ACK, sequence wrap, invalid ACK, zero window, out-of-order ranges and duplicate FIN.
Reviewed reset injection, SYN floods, listener close, timer cancellation races, tuple reuse, zero-copy pins, orphan pressure, CPU hotplug and namespace teardown.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Identity, incarnation, sequence, handshake, queue, timer, reset, close, memory and teardown boundaries receive distinct treatment.

evidence: Traced active and passive handshake, request admission, established publication, accept queueing, send and receive state, timers, half-close, TIME-WAIT and reclamation.
Verified protected lookup, precharged admission, modular guards, transactional promotion, single timer ownership, directional close and dependency-ordered teardown.
invariant_checking.notes: The chapter treats listener, request, established, file-owned, orphan, queued, timer-owned and TIME-WAIT representations as coupled but independently owned state.

evidence: Reviewed tuple lookup, incarnations, ISNs, active and passive open, cookies, segment acceptability, sequence wrap, queues, timers, close, reset and TIME-WAIT.
Constructed counterexamples for tuple-as-incarnation, hash-hit-as-lifetime, ACK-as-peer-consumption, FIN-as-bidirectional-close and timer-cancel-as-callback-impossibility.
proof_review.notes: The chapter supplies reusable connection-state obligations, not a formal proof of TCP, Linux, a transport implementation, network path, peer or application.

evidence: Audited uses of listened, requested, established, accepted, sent, acknowledged, received, closed, reset, timed out, unhashed and reclaimed.
Confirmed standards rules, Linux behavior, abstract models, recommendations, tests and assurance claims remain separately scoped.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Local send acceptance is not labeled peer receipt, transport ACK is not labeled application consumption, tuple match is not labeled incarnation validity and close is not labeled immediate reclamation.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/OS-076/report.json records source, expected and actual output, stderr, exit status, toolchain and environment for the guarded connection-transition model.
Reviewed required namespace, tuple, listener, sequence, queue, timer, route, CPU, workload, fault, trace and application evidence.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The passing toy establishes one abstract transition chain only; it provides no evidence for TCP conformance, Linux lifetime safety, attack resistance, teardown or performance.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed connection state as a guarded and resource-accounted object graph joining protocol sequence semantics to lookup, queues, timers, application ownership and reclamation.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed current connection mechanisms as implementable concerns, including request promotion, accept admission, cookies, modular sequence checks, timer generations, half-close, TIME-WAIT and teardown. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from identity and incarnations through active/passive open, cookies, sequence processing, send/receive queues, timers, close, reset, accounting and testing, followed by twelve obligations, sixteen trade-offs, twenty-five misconceptions, ten examples and five complete exercises.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external operating-systems academic, IETF, Linux networking, transport-implementation, network-operator, security, performance, independent-verification or certification review is claimed.
